title: Investment Manager Selection
hook: Picking a manager is hypothesis testing: is there real skill? Get the error type wrong and you fire winners or hire pretenders.

keyterms.def: Structured search: universe definition, quantitative screening, and qualitative due diligence to choose a manager fitting the mandate.
Rejecting a true null of no skill: hiring or keeping a manager who actually has no genuine skill (false positive).
Failing to reject false null: firing or not hiring a manager who truly does have skill (false negative).
Regresses fund returns on index returns to infer style exposures; cheap, uniform, but backward-looking and imprecise.
Aggregates actual portfolio holdings to characterize style; current and precise but data-heavy and less comparable.
A manager's actual exposures moving away from the stated mandate over time, detectable via style analysis.
Review of back-office controls, custody, compliance, valuation, and counterparties to assess non-investment risk.
Fee tied to returns above a hurdle, often with a high-water mark, aligning manager pay with client outcomes.

body: The goal of manager selection is not simply to find the best past performer but to identify a manager whose expected future results, adjusted for risk and cost, best fit a specific mandate. Strong past returns are noisy and easily produced by luck, so selection combines statistical evidence with judgment.

The process has three linked stages. First, the universe is defined by the mandate (asset class, style, constraints). Second, a quantitative stage screens performance, risk, and style consistency. Third, a qualitative stage conducts due diligence on philosophy, process, people, and operations. Quantitative work says what happened; qualitative work explains why and whether it is repeatable.

callout.label: FIT OVER FAME
callout.text: Selection optimizes mandate fit and repeatable skill, not headline returns. A top performer that drifts from the mandate is a poor selection.

sections.h: 2. Type I vs Type II Errors
body: Frame hiring as a hypothesis test where the null is the manager has no skill. A Type I error is wrongly rejecting a true null: you conclude skill exists and hire (or retain) a manager who in fact has none. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null: you conclude no skill and reject (or fire) a manager who truly does have skill.

Both errors carry real costs. Type I brings underperformance, fees, and eventual disruption from replacing the manager. Type II brings the opportunity cost of forgone alpha plus the transaction and search costs of switching. Tightening standards to cut one error type typically raises the other, so committees must weigh the relative costs rather than eliminate errors.
sections.formula:
H0: no skill
Type I  = reject true H0 = HIRE a no-skill manager
Type II = accept false H0 = FIRE a skilled manager

callout.label: DON'T FLIP
callout.text: Type I = hiring the pretender (false positive on skill). Type II = firing the star (false negative). Anchor to the null 'no skill' to avoid reversing them.

body: RBSA regresses a fund's historical returns against a set of style indices, constraining the coefficients to be non-negative and to sum to one, so they read as an effective style mix. It needs only a return series, applies uniformly across managers, and is inexpensive and quick to run.

Its weaknesses follow from using only returns. It is backward-looking, blends exposures over the estimation window, and can lag real shifts or misread a manager whose true holdings are unusual. Low explanatory power (R2) or unstable coefficients can flag style drift or benchmark mismatch.
sections.formula:
r_fund = a + b_1*I_1 + ... + b_n*I_n + e
subject to: b_i >= 0 and sum(b_i) = 1

body: HBSA classifies the actual securities in the portfolio (by size, value/growth metrics, sector, credit, duration) and aggregates them to a current style profile. Because it uses positions, it is forward-consistent and precise, detects drift faster, and pinpoints the sources of exposure.

The trade-offs are practical: it demands frequent, detailed holdings data that may be disclosed with a lag, is computationally heavier, and depends on a consistent classification scheme, making cross-manager comparison harder. In practice RBSA and HBSA are complementary checks.

callout.label: PAIR THEM
callout.text: RBSA is cheap and uniform but stale; HBSA is precise and current but data-hungry. Agreement between them raises confidence; divergence flags a problem.

body: Due diligence tests whether observed results reflect a sound, repeatable approach. Review the investment philosophy (the economic rationale for the edge), the process (idea generation, portfolio construction, risk controls, sell discipline, and whether it is actually followed), and the people (experience, depth, incentives, ownership, and key-person risk).

Operations cover the non-investment risks that can be catastrophic: custody and asset safekeeping, independent valuation, compliance and controls, trading and counterparties, technology, and business viability. A brilliant strategy on a weak operational platform is not investable, so operational red flags can veto an otherwise strong candidate.

callout.label: OPS CAN VETO
callout.text: The four P's plus operations. Weak controls, self-valuation, or key-person risk can disqualify a manager regardless of returns.

body: Fee structure shapes incentives. An ad valorem (assets-under-management) fee is predictable for clients but rewards asset gathering over performance. A performance-based fee pays a base plus a share of returns above a hurdle, better aligning pay with results but potentially encouraging risk-taking.

Alignment tools temper that risk. A high-water mark stops the manager from earning incentive fees on gains that merely recover prior losses. A hurdle rate requires beating a threshold before sharing. Symmetric (fulcrum) fees that penalize underperformance, along with fee caps and the manager investing personal capital, further align interests. Lower, simpler fees also raise the after-cost return the client keeps.
sections.formula:
Perf fee = base + k * max(0, R - hurdle)
High-water mark: incentive paid only on new peak NAV

callout.label: NET IS KING
callout.text: Compare managers on expected net-of-fee, risk-adjusted return. High-water marks and hurdles protect clients from paying for recovered losses.

flow: Define the universe from the mandate (asset class, style, constraints)
Screen quantitatively: risk-adjusted returns, consistency, style analysis (RBSA + HBSA)
Run qualitative due diligence on philosophy, process, people, and operations
Weigh Type I vs Type II error costs when deciding to hire, retain, or fire
Assess fees and alignment; compare candidates on net-of-fee, risk-adjusted terms
Select, then monitor for style drift and mandate fit over time

quiz.q: Treating 'the manager has no skill' as the null hypothesis, which mistake is hiring a manager who genuinely has no skill?
o: Type I error
Type II error
Sampling error
quiz.e: Hiring a truly unskilled manager wrongly rejects a true null (no skill), which is a Type I error, a false positive.

quiz.q: Which mistake is firing (or not hiring) a manager who truly does possess skill?
o: Type I error
Type II error
Anchoring error
quiz.e: Rejecting a manager who actually has skill fails to reject a false null, a Type II error, a false negative that forgoes real alpha.

quiz.q: A key advantage of return-based style analysis over holdings-based analysis is that it:
o: Detects style drift almost instantly
Requires only a return series and is cheap and uniform
Pinpoints the exact securities driving exposure
quiz.e: RBSA needs only returns, making it inexpensive and uniformly applicable; detecting drift instantly and pinpointing securities are HBSA strengths.

quiz.q: Compared with RBSA, holdings-based style analysis primarily offers:
o: Lower data requirements
Greater current precision and faster drift detection
Easier cross-manager comparability
quiz.e: HBSA uses actual positions, giving current, precise exposures and quicker drift detection, at the cost of heavier data needs and weaker comparability.

quiz.q: Which item belongs to operational (rather than investment) due diligence?
o: The economic rationale behind the manager's edge
Independent valuation and custody of assets
The portfolio construction and sell discipline
quiz.e: Custody and independent valuation are operational controls; rationale and construction are part of philosophy and process.

quiz.q: A high-water mark in a performance fee primarily ensures that the manager:
o: Earns incentive fees only on gains above the prior peak NAV
Receives a fixed fee regardless of performance
Beats a market index every quarter
quiz.e: A high-water mark blocks incentive fees on gains that only recover previous losses, so the client does not pay twice for the same performance.

quiz.q: Why is a manager's strong past return, by itself, a weak selection criterion?
o: It is always fabricated
It can arise from luck and may reflect style drift, not repeatable skill
Regulators prohibit using returns
quiz.e: Past returns are noisy; luck or off-mandate drift can produce them, so selection also needs style consistency and qualitative evidence of repeatable skill.

quiz.q: Increasing the evidentiary bar required to hire a manager will most likely:
o: Eliminate both Type I and Type II errors
Reduce Type I errors but raise Type II errors
Reduce Type II errors but raise Type I errors
quiz.e: A stricter bar rejects more candidates, cutting false hires (Type I) but rejecting more genuinely skilled managers (Type II); the two errors trade off.
